paragraphs: Priam replied, “If you really are a squire of Achilles son of Peleus, tell me the whole truth. Is my son still beside the ships? Or has Achilles hacked him limb from limb and thrown him to his dogs?”

“Sir,” said the slayer of Argus, who was his guide and guardian, “no dogs or vultures have eaten him. He is simply lying at the tents, by Achilles’s ship. Twelve days have now passed while he lay there, and his flesh has not wasted away, nor have the worms eaten him, though they feed on men killed in war. Each daybreak Achilles drags him cruelly around the tomb of his dear comrade, but this does no harm to the body. You should come and see for yourself how he lies there fresh as dew, with the blood washed off, and every one of his wounds closed, though many men drove their spears into him. That is how well the blessed gods have looked after your brave son, because he was dear to them beyond measure.”

The old man was comforted by this. He said, “My son, it is a good thing to have given the immortals their due offerings. As surely as he was my son, he never forgot the gods who hold Olympus, and now they repay him for it even in death. So accept this fine cup from me. Protect me, and with the help of the gods lead me until I reach the tent of the son of Peleus.”

The slayer of Argus, his guide and guardian, answered, “Sir, you are testing me and taking advantage of my youth, but you will not persuade me. You are offering me gifts behind the back of Achilles, whom I fear. I think it a great wrong to cheat him, in case something bad happens to me for it. But as your guide I would go with you all the way to Argos itself, and I would guard you so carefully, by sea or by land, that nobody would attack you out of contempt for the one who was with you.”

The bringer of good luck then jumped onto the chariot. He took the whip and reins and put new spirit into the mules and horses. When they reached the trench and the wall in front of the ships, the guards there had just been eating their suppers. The slayer of Argus put them all into a deep sleep. He then pulled back the bolts to open the gates, and brought Priam inside, along with the treasure on his wagon. Before long they came to the tall dwelling of the son of Peleus. The Myrmidons had cut pine for it and built it for their king. When it was built, they had roofed it with coarse tussock grass mown from the plain, and all around it they had made a large courtyard, fenced with stakes set close together. The gate was held shut by a single bolt of pine. It took three men to push it into place and three to pull it back and open the gate, but Achilles could draw it by himself. Hermes opened the gate for the old man and brought in the treasure that Priam was taking for the son of Peleus. Then he jumped down from the chariot to the ground and said, “Sir, I am the immortal Hermes. I came with you because my father sent me to escort you. Now I will leave you, and I will not go into the presence of Achilles. It might anger him if a god were seen helping mortals so openly. Go in yourself and clasp the knees of the son of Peleus. Beg him in the name of his father, his lovely mother and his son, and you may move him.”

With these words Hermes returned to high Olympus. Priam jumped down from his chariot to the ground and left Idaeus where he was, to look after the mules and horses. The old man walked straight into the house where Achilles, beloved of the gods, was sitting. He found him there, with his men sitting apart from him. Only two of them, the hero Automedon and Alcimus of the race of Ares, were busy attending to him. He had only just finished eating and drinking, and the table was still in place. King Priam came in without being noticed, went right up to Achilles, and clasped his knees. He kissed those dreadful, murderous hands that had killed so many of his sons.

When a cruel blow of fate has made a man kill someone in his own country, and he has to flee to a great man’s protection in a land of strangers, everyone who sees him is amazed. Achilles was amazed in just that way when he saw Priam. The others looked at one another in amazement too. Then Priam begged Achilles, saying, “Think of your father, Achilles, you who are like the gods. He is as old as I am, standing on the sad threshold of old age. Perhaps his neighbors are harassing him, and there is no one to keep war and ruin away from him. Yet when he hears that you are still alive, he is glad, and every day he hopes to see his dear son come home to him from Troy. But I am a wretched man. I had the bravest sons in all Troy, and not one of them is left. I had fifty sons when the Achaeans came here. Nineteen of them came from a single womb, and the others were borne to me by the women of my household. Fierce Ares has laid most of them low. Hector was the only one left, the guardian of our city and of ourselves, and you killed him not long ago. That is why I have now come to the ships of the Achaeans, to ransom his body from you with a great ransom. Fear the anger of heaven, Achilles. Think of your own father and pity me. I am more pitiable than he, because I have done what no man on earth has done before me. I have raised to my lips the hand of the man who killed my son.”

So Priam spoke, and Achilles ached with longing as he thought of his father. He took the old man’s hand and gently pushed him back. The two of them wept bitterly. Priam lay at Achilles’s feet and wept for Hector, and Achilles wept sometimes for his father and sometimes for Patroclus, until the house was full of their crying. But when Achilles had had enough of grief and the bitterness of his sorrow had left him, he rose from his seat. In pity for the old man’s white hair and beard, he lifted him up by the hand. Then he said, “Unhappy man, you have dared a great deal. How could you come alone to the ships of the Achaeans, into the presence of the man who has killed so many of your brave sons? Your courage must be iron. Sit down on this seat now. Whatever our grief, we will let our sorrows lie quiet in our hearts, because weeping gets us nowhere. The immortals feel no care, yet the lot they spin for men is full of sorrow. On the floor of Zeus’s palace stand two urns, one filled with evil gifts and the other with good ones. The man for whom Zeus, the lord of thunder, mixes the gifts he sends will meet with good fortune at one time and evil at another. But the man to whom Zeus sends only evil gifts will be pointed at with scorn. Hunger will hound him to the ends of the world, and he will wander the face of the earth, honored by neither gods nor men. That is what happened to Peleus. From his birth the gods gave him every good thing. He ruled the Myrmidons and surpassed all men in prosperity and wealth, and though he was mortal, they gave him a goddess for his wife. But heaven sent him misfortune too. No line of royal children was born to him in his house. He has one son only, who is doomed to die before his time. I cannot look after him now that he is growing old, because I must stay here at Troy to bring ruin to you and your children. And you also, Priam, I have heard were happy once. They say that in wealth and in number of children you surpassed everyone in Lesbos, the realm of Makar to the north, in Phrygia farther inland, and among the people along the great Hellespont. But since the day the dwellers in heaven brought this evil on you, there has been war and slaughter around your city without end. Bear up under it, and let your sorrow have some pauses. You will gain nothing by mourning your brave son. You cannot raise him from the dead, and before you do, you will suffer yet another sorrow.”

Priam answered, “O king, do not tell me to sit while Hector is still lying uncared for in your tents. Accept the great ransom I have brought you, and give him to me at once so that I can look at him. May you enjoy the ransom and reach your own land safely, since you have let me live and see the light of the sun.”

Achilles looked at him sternly and said, “Do not provoke me any more, sir. I myself intend to give up Hector’s body. My mother, the daughter of the old man of the sea, came to me from Zeus to tell me to hand it over to you. And I know well, Priam, and you cannot hide it from me, that some god brought you to the ships of the Achaeans. No man, however strong and in his prime, would dare to come into our camp otherwise. He could not get past our guards unseen, and he could not draw the bolt of my gates so easily. So do not stir me up further, or I may sin against the word of Zeus and refuse to receive you in my tents, suppliant though you are.”

The old man was afraid of him and obeyed. Then the son of Peleus sprang out through the door of his house like a lion. He did not go alone. His two squires, Automedon and Alcimus, went with him. Now that Patroclus was dead, he valued these two above all his other comrades. They unyoked the horses and mules, and told Priam’s herald and attendant to sit inside the house. They lifted the ransom for Hector’s body down from the wagon, but left two mantles and a fine shirt for Achilles to wrap the body in when it was given back to be taken home. Then Achilles called to his servants and told them to wash the body and anoint it. First he had it taken to a place where Priam could not see it. He was afraid that Priam, seeing it, might break out in the bitterness of his grief and enrage him, so that he would kill the old man and sin against the word of Zeus. When the servants had washed and anointed the body and wrapped it in a fair shirt and mantle, Achilles himself lifted it onto a bier, and he and his men laid it on the wagon. As he did so he cried aloud and called on his dear comrade by name. “Do not be angry with me, Patroclus,” he said, “if you learn, even in the house of Hades, that I gave Hector back to his father for a ransom. It was not an unworthy one, and I will share it with you fairly.”

Achilles then went back into the tent and sat down again in the richly inlaid seat he had risen from. It stood by the wall at right angles to the one Priam was sitting against. “Sir,” he said, “your son is laid on his bier and ransomed as you wished. You will see him when you take him away at daybreak. For now, let us get our supper ready. Even lovely Niobe had to think about eating, though her twelve children, six daughters and six strong sons, had all been killed in her house. Apollo killed the sons with arrows from his silver bow, as a punishment to Niobe, and Artemis killed the daughters, because Niobe had boasted against Leto. She said that Leto had borne only two children, while she herself had borne many. So the two killed the many. For nine days they lay in their blood and there was no one to bury them, because the son of Cronus had turned the people to stone. On the tenth day the gods of heaven buried them themselves, and then Niobe, worn out with weeping, ate. They say that somewhere among the rocks on the mountain pastures of Sipylus, where the nymphs who haunt the river Achelous have their home, she lives on as stone, and still nurses the sorrows the gods sent her. So, noble sir, let the two of us eat now. You can weep for your dear son later, when you carry him back to Ilium, and he will cost you many tears.”

With this Achilles sprang up from his seat and killed a sheep with silvery white wool. His followers skinned it and prepared it in the proper way. They cut the meat carefully into smaller pieces, put them on spits, and drew them off again when they were well roasted. Automedon brought bread in fair baskets and served it around the table, while Achilles dealt out the meat, and they reached for the good things set before them. When they had had enough to eat and drink, Priam, descendant of Dardanus, looked in wonder at the strength and beauty of Achilles, who was like a god to see. Achilles in turn wondered at Priam as he listened to him and looked at his noble presence. When they had looked their fill at each other, Priam spoke first. “Now, O king,” he said, “take me to my bed, so that we may lie down and enjoy the blessed gift of sleep. My eyes have not closed once since the day your hands took my son’s life. I have wallowed without stopping in the mud of my stable yard, moaning and brooding over my countless sorrows. Now I have also eaten bread and drunk wine. Until now I had tasted nothing.”

As he spoke, Achilles told his men and the women servants to set up beds in the room in the gatehouse. They were to make them with good red rugs, spread coverlets on top, and put woolen cloaks there for Priam and Idaeus to wear. So the maids went out with a torch and got the two beds ready in great haste. Then Achilles said to Priam, half laughing, “Dear sir, you must sleep outside. One of the counselors who regularly come to advise with me might see you here in the darkness of the fleeting night and tell Agamemnon. That could delay the handing over of the body. Now tell me, and tell me truly, how many days do you want for the funeral rites of noble Hector? Tell me, so that I can keep away from fighting and hold back the army.”

Priam answered, “Since you are letting me bury my noble son with all the proper rites, Achilles, do as I ask and I will be grateful. You know how we are shut up inside our city. It is a long way for us to fetch wood from the mountain, and the people are afraid. So we will mourn Hector in my house for nine days. On the tenth day we will bury him, and there will be a public feast in his honor. On the eleventh we will build a mound over his ashes, and on the twelfth, if we must, we will fight.”
Achilles answered, “King Priam, everything will be as you have said. I will hold back our fighting for as long as you have named.”

As he spoke he took the old man by the right wrist, as a sign that he should have no fear. So Priam and his attendant slept there in the forecourt, their minds full of thought. Achilles lay in an inner room of the house, with fair Briseis beside him.

Now gods and mortals alike lay fast asleep through the whole night. Only Hermes, the bringer of good luck, could not be taken by sleep. He was thinking the whole time how to get King Priam away from the ships without being seen by the strong force of sentries. He hovered over Priam’s head and said, “Sir, now that Achilles has spared your life, you seem to have no fear of sleeping among your enemies. You have paid a great ransom and received the body of your son. If you were alive and a prisoner, the sons you left at home would have to give three times as much to free you. And so it would be if Agamemnon and the other Achaeans found out you were here.”

When the old man heard this, he was afraid and woke his servant. Hermes yoked their horses and mules and drove them quickly through the army, so that no one saw them. When they came to the ford of eddying Xanthus, begotten of immortal Zeus, Hermes went back to high Olympus, and saffron-robed Dawn began to break over all the land. Priam and Idaeus drove on toward the city, crying out and groaning, and the mules drew the body of Hector. No one, man or woman, saw them until Cassandra, as fair as golden Aphrodite, standing on Pergamus, caught sight of her dear father in his chariot, with his servant, who was the city’s herald, beside him. Then she saw the man lying on the bier behind the mules. With a loud cry she went about the city, saying, “Come here, Trojans, men and women, and look at Hector. If you ever rejoiced to see him coming home from battle while he was alive, look now at the man who was the glory of our city and of all our people.”

At this, not a man or woman was left in the city, so great a sorrow came over them. Close to the gates they met Priam as he was bringing in the body. Hector’s wife and his mother were the first to mourn him. They rushed toward the wagon and laid their hands on his head, while the crowd stood weeping around them. They would have stayed before the gates weeping and lamenting all day until the sun went down, if Priam had not spoken to them from the chariot. He said, “Make way for the mules to pass. Afterward, when I have taken the body home, you may weep as much as you like.”

At this the people stood aside and made way for the wagon. When they had carried the body into the house, they laid it on a bed and seated singers around it to lead the dirge. Then the women joined in with the sad music of their lament. Andromache led their wailing, foremost of them all, holding the head of mighty Hector in her arms. “Husband,” she cried, “you have died young and left me a widow in your house. The child we ill-starred parents have is still only a boy, and I fear he may not reach manhood. Before he can, our city will be destroyed and overthrown, because you who watched over it are gone, you who saved it and guarded our wives and children. Our women will be carried off to the ships as captives, and I with them. And you, my child, who will be with me, will be put to some unseemly tasks, working for a cruel master. Or perhaps some Achaean will hurl you from our walls to a miserable death, to avenge a brother, son or father whom Hector killed. Many of them have bitten the dust at his hands, because your father’s hand in battle was no light one. That is why the people mourn him. Hector, you have left unspeakable sorrow to your parents, and my own grief is greatest of all. You did not stretch out your arms to embrace me as you lay dying, and you said no words to me that I could have kept in my mind as I weep night and day for evermore.”

She wept bitterly as she spoke, and the women joined in her lament. Hecuba in her turn took up the cry of woe. “Hector,” she cried, “you are the dearest to me of all my children. As long as you were alive the gods loved you well, and even in death they have not forgotten you entirely. When Achilles took any other son of mine, he would sell him across the seas, to Samos, Imbrus or rugged Lemnos. And when he had killed you too with his sword, he dragged you many times around the tomb of his comrade, though that could not bring his comrade back to life. Yet here you lie, fresh as dew and beautiful as someone Apollo has killed with his painless arrows.”

So she too spoke through her tears, with bitter moaning. Then Helen took up the lament for the third time. “Hector,” she said, “you are the dearest to me of all my brothers-in-law. I am the wife of Paris, who brought me here to Troy, and I wish I had died before he did that. Twenty years have now passed since I left my home and came from over the sea, and in all that time I have never heard one insulting or unkind word from you. When someone else scolded me, one of your brothers or sisters or your brothers’ wives, or my mother-in-law (Priam was as kind to me as if he were my own father), you would stop them and correct them with gentle, kindly words. So my tears flow both for you and for my unhappy self. There is no one else in Troy who is kind to me. Everyone shrinks and shudders as they go by me.”

She wept as she spoke, and the vast crowd gathered around her joined in her lament. Then King Priam spoke to them. He said, “Bring wood to the city, Trojans, and do not fear any cunning ambush by the Argives. When Achilles sent me away from the ships, he gave me his word that they would not attack us until the morning of the twelfth day.”

At once they yoked their oxen and mules and gathered in front of the city. For nine days they brought in great heaps of wood. On the morning of the tenth day, with many tears, they carried brave Hector out, laid his dead body on top of the pile, and set fire to it. Then, when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared on the eleventh day, the people gathered again around the pyre of mighty Hector. When they were all there, they first put out the fire with wine wherever it was still burning. Then his brothers and comrades, with many bitter tears, gathered his white bones. They wrapped them in soft purple robes and laid them in a golden urn, which they placed in a grave and covered with large stones set close together. Then they hurriedly built a barrow over it, posting guards on every side in case the Achaeans attacked before they had finished. When they had heaped up the barrow, they went back into the city. They all assembled and held a grand feast in the house of Priam their king.
That is how they celebrated the funeral of Hector, tamer of horses.
